claims.text: Tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloys are relevant candidate materials for plasma-facing fusion applications.
The proposed intervention is addition of approximately 2–5 at.% Ti to an additively manufactured tungsten-based RHEA.
The baseline W–Ta–Cr–V alloy has a largely homogeneous BCC microstructure with no deliberate second-phase precipitates.
Adding 2–5 at.% Ti in the presence of trace carbon during additive manufacturing will produce TiC nanoprecipitates in situ.
The in situ TiC nanoprecipitates will be coherent with the BCC matrix and evenly dispersed.
The TiC nanoprecipitates will provide sites for irradiation-defect recombination.
The TiC nanoprecipitates will act as sinks for helium atoms.
Defect recombination and helium trapping at the precipitates will limit helium-bubble growth and coalescence.
Coherent nanoprecipitate interfaces reduce stress concentrations that could otherwise initiate premature cracking.
Coherent nanoprecipitates can preserve a favorable combination of strength and tensile ductility in tungsten refractory HEAs.
The Ti-modified alloy will have a statistically significant reduction in average helium-bubble size and density relative to the Ti-free baseline.
The Ti-modified alloy will exhibit a lower irradiation-induced hardening fraction than the Ti-free baseline.
The Ti-modified alloy will maintain or improve tensile strength and ductility relative to the baseline after irradiation.
The unmodified tungsten-based RHEA develops larger helium bubbles and greater irradiation-induced hardening under the stated irradiation conditions.
Approximately 200 keV helium-ion irradiation at 900 °C and application-typical fluence represents reactor-relevant testing for the proposed effect.
The beneficial effect depends on an additive-manufacturing route that successfully produces the coherent nanoprecipitates.
Variations in Ti content, carbon availability, or processing parameters could change the effectiveness of the intervention.
Additively manufactured compositionally complex refractory alloys can be produced, and greater compositional complexity may improve helium-irradiation tolerance when elemental segregation is avoided.
